notes:
1. Human Development — Meaning

  • Human development means expansion of people's capabilities, choices and opportunities.
  • It focuses on whether people can live long, healthy, knowledgeable and productive lives.
  • Economic growth provides resources, but human development examines how those resources improve actual quality of life.
📌 Must-Memorise

Economic Growth → Resources

Human Development → Capabilities + Quality of Life

2. Human Development — Major Dimensions

Important dimensions include:

  • Health.
  • Education.
  • Income.
  • Nutrition.
  • Housing.
  • Employment.
  • Gender equality.
  • Basic services.
  • Social security.

3. Economic Development vs Human Development

Economic development focuses strongly on:

  • Production.
  • Income.
  • Investment.
  • Structural transformation.

Human development focuses on:

  • Health.
  • Education.
  • Opportunities.
  • Capabilities.
  • Quality of life.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Economic Growth ≠ Human Development

4. Human Development Index — HDI

  • HDI stands for Human Development Index.
  • It was developed within the UNDP human-development framework.
  • It combines achievements in three basic dimensions.
📌 Must-Memorise

HDI → Health + Education + Standard of Living

5. HDI — Health Dimension

  • The standard HDI health indicator is Life Expectancy at Birth.
📌 Must-Memorise

HDI Health → Life Expectancy at Birth

6. HDI — Education Dimension

The global HDI education dimension uses:

  • Mean Years of Schooling.
  • Expected Years of Schooling.
📌 Must-Memorise

HDI Education → MYS + EYS

7. HDI — Income Dimension

  • The standard-of-living dimension uses Gross National Income per capita under UNDP methodology.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Global HDI Income Measure → GNI per Capita

Not State GSDP Directly

8. HDI — Composite Nature

  • HDI combines its three dimensions using a geometric-mean methodology.
  • It is therefore a composite index rather than a single social indicator.

9. HDI vs MPI vs SDG Index

  • HDI → Health + Education + Income.
  • MPI → Multiple household deprivations.
  • SDG Index → Broader Sustainable Development Goal performance.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

HDI ≠ MPI ≠ SDG Index

10. Tamil Nadu — Human Development Dashboard

Tamil Nadu's human-development performance can be examined through:

  • Per capita output.
  • Poverty.
  • MPI.
  • Literacy.
  • Higher education.
  • Life expectancy.
  • IMR.
  • Fertility.
  • Immunisation.
  • Nutrition.
  • Water.
  • Sanitation.
  • Electricity.
  • Gender participation.
  • Employment.
  • Urbanisation.
  • SDG performance.

11. Why One Indicator Is Not Enough

  • High per capita income cannot fully compensate for poor nutrition or weak health access.
  • High literacy alone does not guarantee high educational quality.
  • Human development therefore requires multiple indicators.
📌 Must-Memorise

Human Development → Economic + Social + Capability Indicators

12. Tamil Nadu — Per Capita GSDP

According to the supplied NITI Aayog profile:

  • Tamil Nadu nominal per capita GSDP in 2021–22 was approximately ₹2,70,629.
  • The corresponding all-India figure was approximately ₹1,71,498.
📌 Must-Memorise

TN Per Capita GSDP 2021–22 → ₹2.71 Lakh Approx.

13. Why Per Capita Income Matters

Higher per capita income can support:

  • Consumption.
  • Savings.
  • Housing.
  • Education.
  • Health expenditure.
  • Government revenue capacity.

14. Per Capita Income — Limitation

  • High average income does not guarantee equal distribution.
  • Public-service access may also differ between groups and regions.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

High Per Capita Income ≠ Automatically High Human Development

15. Per Capita GSDP vs HDI Income Measure

  • Per capita GSDP is useful for State economic analysis.
  • Standard global HDI uses GNI per capita.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Per Capita GSDP ≠ HDI Income Indicator

16. Tamil Nadu — Multidimensional Poverty

According to NITI Aayog:

  • 2015–16 → 4.76%.
  • 2019–21 → 2.20%.
📌 Must-Memorise

TN MPI → 4.76% to 2.20%

17. Tamil Nadu — Extrapolated MPI 2022–23

  • The supplied source gives an extrapolated estimate of approximately 1.43% for 2022–23.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

1.43% → Extrapolated Estimate

Not a Separate Direct NFHS Headcount

18. Why MPI Matters for Tamil Nadu

Multidimensional poverty captures deprivation in:

  • Health.
  • Education.
  • Living standards.

Therefore poverty reduction should be assessed through:

Income

  • Education
  • Health
  • Housing
  • Basic Services

19. Tamil Nadu — Literacy Rate

  • Tamil Nadu's literacy rate in Census 2011 was approximately 80.1%.
  • The corresponding all-India figure was about 73% in the source.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tamil Nadu Literacy — Census 2011 → 80.1%

20. Literacy — Data Rule

  • The 80.1% figure is a Census 2011 figure.
  • It should not be presented as a 2026 literacy estimate.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Census 2011 Literacy ≠ Current Census Estimate

21. Literacy — Human Development Role

Literacy supports:

  • Employment.
  • Health awareness.
  • Financial inclusion.
  • Political participation.
  • Digital access.
  • Women's empowerment.

22. Literacy vs Educational Quality

  • Literacy reflects basic educational attainment.
  • It does not directly measure school completion, learning quality or occupational skills.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Literacy ≠ Educational Quality

23. Tamil Nadu — Higher-Education GER

According to AISHE 2020–21 data cited in the source:

  • Tamil Nadu higher-education GER for ages 18–23 was 46.9%.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tamil Nadu Higher-Education GER → 46.9%

24. GER — Meaning

  • GER stands for Gross Enrolment Ratio.
  • It measures enrolment relative to the population in the corresponding official age group.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

High GER ≠ Automatically High Education Quality

25. Tamil Nadu — Colleges per Population

  • The source reports 40 colleges per 100,000 persons aged 18–23 for the cited higher-education reference period.

26. Tamil Nadu — Higher-Education Gender Parity Index

  • Tamil Nadu's higher-education Gender Parity Index was 1.07 in the AISHE 2020–21 data cited.
📌 Must-Memorise

Higher-Education GPI → 1.07

27. Gender Parity Index — Meaning

  • A GPI close to 1 indicates broadly similar female and male participation.
  • A value above 1 means the female-to-male ratio is higher for that specific indicator.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

GPI Above 1 ≠ Complete Gender Equality Everywhere

28. Higher Education — Human Development Role

Higher education supports:

  • Skilled employment.
  • Innovation.
  • Research.
  • Entrepreneurship.
  • Professional services.
  • Social mobility.

29. Tamil Nadu — Life Expectancy

  • The source reports Tamil Nadu's SRS life expectancy at 73.2 years in 2020.
📌 Must-Memorise

TN Life Expectancy 2020 → 73.2 Years

30. Tamil Nadu — Infant Mortality Rate

  • Tamil Nadu's SRS IMR in 2020 was 13 per 1,000 live births.
📌 Must-Memorise

TN SRS IMR 2020 → 13

31. Why IMR Is Important

IMR reflects:

  • Maternal health.
  • Nutrition.
  • Newborn care.
  • Immunisation.
  • Sanitation.
  • Health-system access.
📌 Must-Memorise

IMR → Major Human-Development Outcome Indicator

32. SRS vs NFHS — IMR Difference

The source records:

  • SRS 2020 IMR → 13.
  • NFHS 2019–21 IMR → 18.6.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

SRS IMR ≠ NFHS IMR

Always Mention Source and Reference Period

33. Tamil Nadu — Full Immunisation

  • The source reports 89.2% full immunisation for the specified NFHS age group in 2019–21.
📌 Must-Memorise

TN Full Immunisation → 89.2%

34. Health Infrastructure vs Health Outcome

  • The number of hospitals alone does not prove strong health performance.
  • Human-development analysis should examine actual outcomes.
📌 Must-Memorise

Infrastructure → Services → Outcomes

35. Tamil Nadu — Total Fertility Rate

  • Tamil Nadu's TFR was 1.8 children per woman in NFHS-5, 2019–21.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tamil Nadu TFR → 1.8

36. Low Fertility — Development Link

Low fertility is often associated with:

  • Female education.
  • Urbanisation.
  • Child survival.
  • Reproductive-health access.
  • Changing family preferences.

37. Fertility Decline — Initial Benefit

Lower fertility can reduce child dependency.

This can allow greater household investment in each child's:

  • Nutrition.
  • Education.
  • Health.

38. Tamil Nadu — Population Ageing

  • Persistently low fertility combined with longer life expectancy contributes to ageing.
  • Tamil Nadu therefore increasingly faces a shift from child dependency towards elderly dependency.
📌 Must-Memorise

Low Fertility + Longer Life → Population Ageing

39. Ageing — Future Human-Development Need

Tamil Nadu will increasingly require:

  • Geriatric health care.
  • Pensions.
  • Long-term care.
  • Accessible infrastructure.
  • Elderly social support.

40. Tamil Nadu — Child Underweight

According to NFHS-5 data cited:

  • 22.0% of children were underweight.
📌 Must-Memorise

TN Underweight Children → 22.0%

41. Tamil Nadu — Child Stunting

  • 25.0% of children were reported as stunted.
📌 Must-Memorise

TN Child Stunting → 25.0%

42. Stunting — Meaning

  • Stunting means low height for age.
  • It generally reflects chronic or long-term nutritional deprivation and related health conditions.

43. Underweight — Meaning

  • Underweight means low weight for age.
  • It can reflect both chronic and acute nutritional problems.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Stunting ≠ Underweight

44. Tamil Nadu — Anaemia

According to the source:

  • Anaemia among children → 57.4%.
  • Anaemia among women → 53.4%.
📌 Must-Memorise

TN Anaemia → Children 57.4 | Women 53.4

45. Anaemia — Meaning

  • Anaemia commonly involves inadequate haemoglobin concentration in blood.
  • Iron deficiency is an important cause, though anaemia can have multiple causes.

46. Tamil Nadu — Human Development Paradox

  • Tamil Nadu can perform strongly on income, education and health while still facing significant malnutrition and anaemia.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Strong Economic Performance ≠ Automatic Elimination of Malnutrition

47. Tamil Nadu — Improved Drinking Water

  • NFHS-5 data cited in the source report 98.6% of households with access to an improved drinking-water source.
📌 Must-Memorise

TN Improved Drinking Water → 98.6%

48. Tamil Nadu — Electricity Access

  • The source reports 99.0% household access to electricity.
📌 Must-Memorise

TN Electricity Access → 99.0%

49. Tamil Nadu — Sanitation Access

  • Sanitation access under the cited NFHS indicator was 71.2% in 2019–21.
📌 Must-Memorise

TN Sanitation Indicator → 71.2%

50. Basic Services — Human Development Link

Water, sanitation and electricity directly influence:

  • Health.
  • Education.
  • Productivity.
  • Women's dignity.
  • Household welfare.
  • Digital access.
📌 Must-Memorise

Basic Infrastructure → Human Capability

51. Improved Water vs Functional Tap

  • An improved drinking-water source is not automatically the same as a functional household tap connection.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Improved Water Source ≠ FHTC

52. Gender and Human Development

Gender development includes:

  • Education.
  • Health.
  • Employment.
  • Income.
  • Safety.
  • Asset ownership.
  • Political participation.

53. Tamil Nadu — Female LFPR

According to the PLFS 2022–23 measure used in the source:

  • Female LFPR for persons aged 15+ was 40.5%.
📌 Must-Memorise

TN Female LFPR → 40.5% in Cited PLFS 2022–23

54. Education–Employment Gender Gap

  • Strong female educational participation does not automatically translate into equally strong labour-market participation.
📌 Must-Memorise

Women's Education → Must Convert into Skills + Employment + Independence

55. Barriers to Women's Employment

Important barriers include:

  • Unpaid care.
  • Safety.
  • Transport.
  • Workplace conditions.
  • Limited suitable jobs.
  • Social expectations.

56. Tamil Nadu — Urbanisation

  • Census 2011 classified approximately 48.4% of Tamil Nadu's population as urban.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tamil Nadu Urban Share — Census 2011 → 48.4%

57. Tamil Nadu — Projected Urban Share

  • The source reports a projected urban share of approximately 53.7% in 2023.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

53.7% → Projection

Not Census 2023

58. Census vs Projection — Urbanisation

  • 48.4% → Census 2011.
  • 53.7% → Projected 2023 share.
📌 Must-Memorise

Census Count ≠ Projection

59. Urbanisation — Human Development Benefits

Urbanisation can improve access to:

  • Employment.
  • Hospitals.
  • Colleges.
  • Markets.
  • Transport.
  • Digital services.

60. Urbanisation — Human Development Challenges

Rapid urban growth can create:

  • Housing shortages.
  • Congestion.
  • Pollution.
  • Waste-management problems.
  • Informal settlements.
  • Infrastructure pressure.
📌 Must-Memorise

Urbanisation + Planning → Opportunity

Urbanisation Without Planning → Pressure

61. Tamil Nadu — Unemployment Rate

  • The NITI Aayog State profile cited in the source reports an unemployment rate of 4.3% for persons aged 15+ under the specified PLFS 2022–23 Usual Status measure.
📌 Must-Memorise

TN UR in Cited PLFS 2022–23 → 4.3%

62. Employment Quality — Human Development Role

Human development depends not just on whether people have jobs, but also on:

  • Wages.
  • Security.
  • Working conditions.
  • Social protection.
  • Productivity.
📌 Must-Memorise

Employment Quantity + Employment Quality → Human Development

63. Tamil Nadu — Social-Sector Expenditure

According to the supplied NITI Aayog fiscal profile for 2022–23:

  • Per capita social-sector expenditure → approximately ₹15,176.
  • Health → approximately ₹2,353 per capita.
  • Education → approximately ₹5,669 per capita.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

These Are Reference-Year Fiscal Indicators, Not Permanent Values

64. Social Spending — Outcome Rule

  • Higher public spending can support better education, health, nutrition and welfare.
  • But spending alone does not guarantee outcomes.
📌 Must-Memorise

Expenditure → Service Delivery → Outcomes

⚠️ TNPSC Trap

More Spending ≠ Automatically Better Human Development

65. District-Level Disparities

  • State averages can hide substantial differences among districts.
  • Human-development outcomes vary because of differences in urbanisation, industry, geography, employment, infrastructure and social composition.
📌 Must-Memorise

State Average ≠ Every District

66. Why District Data Matter

District-level indicators help identify:

  • Development gaps.
  • Vulnerable groups.
  • Infrastructure shortages.
  • Service-delivery weaknesses.

Human development should therefore be examined at:

State

→ District

→ Block

→ Local Level

67. Sustainable Development Goals — SDGs

The SDGs cover areas including:

  • Poverty.
  • Hunger.
  • Health.
  • Education.
  • Gender equality.
  • Water and sanitation.
  • Economic growth.
  • Inequality.
  • Sustainable cities.
  • Environment.

68. Tamil Nadu — SDG India Index

  • Tamil Nadu recorded an SDG India Index composite score of 78 in 2023–24.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tamil Nadu SDG India Index 2023–24 → 78

69. SDG Score vs HDI

  • Tamil Nadu's score of 78 is an SDG India Index score.
  • It is not an HDI value.
  • It is also not an MPI value.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

78 → SDG Score

Not HDI

70. SDGs Directly Linked to Human Development

Important examples:

  • SDG 1 → No Poverty.
  • SDG 2 → Zero Hunger.
  • SDG 3 → Good Health and Well-Being.
  • SDG 4 → Quality Education.
  • SDG 5 → Gender Equality.
  • SDG 6 → Clean Water and Sanitation.

71. Tamil Nadu — Major Human-Development Strengths

Important strengths include:

  • High educational participation.
  • Expanded health access.
  • Relatively low infant mortality.
  • Higher life expectancy.
  • Low fertility.
  • Low multidimensional poverty.
  • Wide basic-service access.
  • High urbanisation.
  • Strong industrial and service sectors.

72. Tamil Nadu — Remaining Human-Development Challenges

Important concerns include:

  • Child malnutrition.
  • Anaemia.
  • Women's employment.
  • Youth employment.
  • Ageing.
  • Urban infrastructure pressures.
  • District disparities.
  • Employment quality.

73. Tamil Nadu — Next-Phase Human Development

The next phase can be understood as:

  • Access → Quality.
  • Basic education → Skills and employability.
  • Basic health → NCD and elderly care.
  • Poverty reduction → Economic mobility.
  • Urbanisation → Sustainable cities.
  • Women's education → Women's economic participation.

74. HDI Memory Chain

  • Health → Life expectancy.
  • Education → Mean years + Expected years of schooling.
  • Income → GNI per capita.

75. Tamil Nadu Education Memory Chain

  • Literacy → 80.1% — Census 2011.
  • Higher-education GER → 46.9%.
  • GPI → 1.07.
  • Colleges → 40 per 100,000 aged 18–23.

76. Tamil Nadu Health Memory Chain

  • Life expectancy → 73.2 years.
  • SRS IMR → 13.
  • TFR → 1.8.
  • Full immunisation → 89.2%.

77. Tamil Nadu Nutrition Memory Chain

  • Underweight → 22.0%.
  • Stunting → 25.0%.
  • Child anaemia → 57.4%.
  • Women anaemia → 53.4%.

78. Tamil Nadu Living-Standard Memory Chain

  • Improved water → 98.6%.
  • Electricity → 99.0%.
  • Sanitation → 71.2%.

79. Tamil Nadu Poverty and Gender Memory Chain

  • MPI 2015–16 → 4.76%.
  • MPI 2019–21 → 2.20%.
  • Extrapolated 2022–23 → 1.43%.
  • Female LFPR → 40.5%.

80. Tamil Nadu Urban and SDG Memory Chain

  • Urban share Census 2011 → 48.4%.
  • Projected 2023 urban share → 53.7%.
  • SDG India Index 2023–24 → 78.

81. TNPSC Traps

  • Human development and economic growth are different.
  • Per capita income alone does not measure human development.
  • HDI has three dimensions.
  • HDI health indicator → Life expectancy.
  • HDI education → Mean and expected years of schooling.
  • HDI income → GNI per capita.
  • HDI and MPI are different.
  • HDI and SDG Index are different.
  • Tamil Nadu's SDG score 78 is not an HDI score.
  • Tamil Nadu literacy 80.1% is Census 2011 data.
  • GER measures participation, not quality.
  • GPI above 1 does not mean complete gender equality.
  • SRS and NFHS mortality figures should not be mixed.
  • IMR is per 1,000 live births.
  • TFR and population growth rate are different.
  • Low TFR can contribute to population ageing.
  • Strong economic performance does not automatically eliminate malnutrition.
  • Stunting and underweight are different.
  • Improved drinking-water source and functional household tap connection are different.
  • Electricity access does not automatically indicate affordability or quality.
  • State averages can hide district disparities.
  • Census data and projections are different.
  • 48.4% urban → Census 2011.
  • 53.7% urban → Projected 2023.
  • MPI 2.20% → 2019–21.
  • MPI 1.43% → Extrapolated 2022–23 estimate.
  • Female educational participation and female labour-force participation are different.
  • Higher public expenditure does not automatically guarantee better outcomes.
  • Chapter 26 focuses on Tamil Nadu's indicators; comparison with other States belongs to Chapter 27.

82. Ultra-Short Memory Chain

  • HDI → Health + Education + Income.
  • Health → Life Expectancy.
  • Education → MYS + EYS.
  • Income → GNI per Capita.
  • TN Per Capita GSDP → ₹2.71 Lakh.
  • TN Literacy → 80.1%.
  • TN GER → 46.9%.
  • TN GPI → 1.07.
  • TN Life Expectancy → 73.2.
  • TN SRS IMR → 13.
  • TN TFR → 1.8.
  • Immunisation → 89.2%.
  • Underweight → 22%.
  • Stunting → 25%.
  • Child Anaemia → 57.4%.
  • Women Anaemia → 53.4%.
  • Water → 98.6%.
  • Electricity → 99%.
  • Sanitation → 71.2%.
  • TN MPI → 2.20%.
  • TN MPI Extrapolated → 1.43%.
  • Female LFPR → 40.5%.
  • Urban Census 2011 → 48.4%.
  • Urban Projection 2023 → 53.7%.
  • SDG Score → 78.

83. Rapid Revision — TNPSC Most Expected

  • Human development means? → Expansion of capabilities, choices and quality of life.
  • Economic growth and human development same? → No.
  • HDI full form? → Human Development Index.
  • HDI developed under? → UNDP human-development framework.
  • HDI dimensions? → Health, Education and Standard of Living.
  • HDI health indicator? → Life expectancy at birth.
  • HDI education indicators? → Mean years of schooling and expected years of schooling.
  • HDI income indicator? → GNI per capita.
  • HDI and MPI same? → No.
  • HDI and SDG Index same? → No.
  • Tamil Nadu nominal per capita GSDP in cited 2021–22 profile? → About ₹2,70,629.
  • Does high per capita income guarantee human development? → No.
  • Tamil Nadu MPI 2015–16? → 4.76%.
  • Tamil Nadu MPI 2019–21? → 2.20%.
  • Tamil Nadu extrapolated MPI 2022–23? → Approximately 1.43%.
  • Is 1.43% a direct NFHS estimate? → No.
  • Tamil Nadu literacy rate? → 80.1%.
  • Literacy reference? → Census 2011.
  • Tamil Nadu higher-education GER? → 46.9%.
  • Higher-education GPI? → 1.07.
  • Colleges per 100,000 persons aged 18–23? → 40.
  • Tamil Nadu life expectancy in cited SRS 2020 data? → 73.2 years.
  • Tamil Nadu SRS IMR in 2020? → 13 per 1,000 live births.
  • NFHS IMR in source? → 18.6.
  • Can SRS and NFHS IMR be mixed? → No.
  • Full immunisation indicator? → 89.2%.
  • Tamil Nadu TFR? → 1.8.
  • Low TFR leads eventually to? → Population ageing.
  • Underweight children? → 22.0%.
  • Stunted children? → 25.0%.
  • Child anaemia? → 57.4%.
  • Women's anaemia? → 53.4%.
  • Improved drinking-water access? → 98.6%.
  • Electricity access? → 99.0%.
  • Sanitation indicator? → 71.2%.
  • Female LFPR in cited PLFS 2022–23? → 40.5%.
  • Does female education automatically imply female employment? → No.
  • Tamil Nadu urbanisation in Census 2011? → 48.4%.
  • Projected urban share for 2023? → 53.7%.
  • Is 53.7% Census 2023 data? → No.
  • Tamil Nadu unemployment rate in cited PLFS 2022–23 measure? → 4.3%.
  • Per capita social-sector expenditure in cited 2022–23 fiscal profile? → About ₹15,176.
  • Tamil Nadu SDG India Index score 2023–24? → 78.
  • Is 78 Tamil Nadu's HDI? → No.
  • Major future challenges? → Nutrition, women's employment, ageing, urban pressure, employment quality and district disparities.
  • Core Tamil Nadu human-development chain? → Income + Education + Health + Nutrition + Basic Services + Employment + Gender + Sustainability.
